traveler: Arthur Ben (the name the corpus uses; his legal name is kept off the atlas at the family's request)
title: The Two Straits and the Apron: a radioman, a medievalist, and the memory theatre folded out of bed sheets
years: dates unestablished: an American twentieth-century life, from the radio room to the mountain at Sewanee
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: The United States, a birth the atlas does not hold
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: no public record and no line of the corpus gives a year or a town; the pin is the geographic center of the United States, a placeholder and nothing else
stops.campa: He is born somewhere in the United States, in a decade the atlas cannot name, to parents whose ashes he will one day ask to be carried in the two front pockets of a funerary apron. The census of the Colegio Invisible enters him as bibliophile and grand master. The queue enters him as librarian and archivist, Oxford medievalist, Navy veteran turned radical pacifist, the author's stepfather. His legal name is withheld at the family's request, and with it every public record that could have been searched under it. Arthur Ben is the name the atlas uses.
suggested_refs: Any US birth index or Navy personnel record obtainable through the NPRC under his legal name, which this atlas does not carry

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, the watch on the receivers
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the rating is given in the corpus, the crossing is reconstruction; no ship, unit, or year is attested
stops.campa: He crosses east as a radio communications technician, a rating that puts a man in a steel room with headphones and a key while the ship above him does the sailing. The traffic comes in code and leaves in code, and the operator is the one aboard who hears everything and is permitted to understand none of it. Joseph Pilates crossed this same water in 1926 beside a woman whose hands were failing, teaching movement in the deck chairs. Ben crosses it listening, and takes up the habit that outlasts the Navy: everything arrives as a sequence, and the sequence has to be kept.
suggested_refs: Deck logs and muster rolls of US Navy vessels transiting the Atlantic in the 1950s, National Archives, College Park

stops.name: Port Said, the gate of the East
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: reconstruction of the only route that joins the two straits he names
stops.campa: The ship enters the canal at Port Said, where Hermann Keyserling entered it in 1911 on the voyage that became the Travel Diary of a Philosopher, and where Ferdinand de Lesseps had cut two seas into one. Ben will be read Keyserling at the end of his life by a stepson not yet born. The convoy moves south at the speed of a man walking. On both banks the desert runs level with the deck, and the radio room keeps its schedules regardless of which country the hull is passing through.
suggested_refs: Suez Canal Authority transit registers for the mid-1950s

stops.name: Bab al-Mandab, the gate of tears
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the strait is named by the dying man, the year is placement only
stops.campa: The Red Sea narrows to eighteen miles between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, and the strait is called the Gate of Tears for the ships it has taken. Ibn Battuta came down this water in 1330 bound for Aden and the Swahili coast. Sixty years after Ben passes through it, dying in a room in Tennessee, this is the first place his speech goes; he names it before he names his own parents. The strait is the hinge of the old world, and a radioman on watch is one of the few aboard awake to see it in the dark.
stops.quote: Amidst his flickering, Ben spoke of his travels through the Straits of Bab al-Mandan and Malacca, the tribes of Yemen and Gaul, and the bloodlines of Abraham.
stops.quote_source: 200_arthur_ben.md, the hospice room at Sewanee (locked essay corpus)
suggested_refs: The Bab al-Mandab strait between Perim and the Djibouti shore

stops.name: Sana'a, the tribes of Yemen
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the essay names Yemen and no town; the pin is Sana'a as a placeholder and is declared as one
stops.campa: The essay names the tribes of Yemen and gives no town, so the atlas sets the pin at Sana'a and says plainly that it is a placeholder. Yemen is where Abu Karib As'ad ruled the Himyarites and, in the Arab tradition, first draped the Kaaba in cloth. It is where Ibn Battuta's road to India began. Whether Ben went ashore, or watched the coast from a ship that never stopped, no record anywhere says. What survives is that the coast entered him and stayed sixty years, and came back out in order when the order of everything else was going.
suggested_refs: The Yemeni Red Sea and Gulf of Aden ports of the 1950s: Hodeidah, Mocha, Aden

stops.name: The Strait of Malacca, the narrow water
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the strait is named by the dying man, the year is placement only
stops.campa: Between Sumatra and the Malay peninsula the sea closes to a channel that every cargo of the East has had to thread. Marco Polo waited out a monsoon on the Sumatran side in 1291. Ibn Battuta crossed to the sultanate of Samudera Pasai in 1345 and found a Shafi'i court at the end of the ocean. Ben's ship goes through under a log nobody has found. Two straits are what he keeps out of a whole naval career, Bab al-Mandab and Malacca, and both are places where the world is forced narrow and everything passing through it can be counted.
suggested_refs: The Malacca strait between One Fathom Bank and Port Klang

stops.name: Samudera Pasai, the end of the ocean
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: inherited pin, standing for the far end of the strait he names; no landfall is attested for Ben
stops.campa: On the northern tip of Sumatra stood the first Muslim sultanate of the archipelago, where Ibn Battuta was received by a sultan who kept jurists at his table and argued law in the Shafi'i manner half a world from Cairo. The atlas keeps the pin because the traveller's strait and the radioman's strait are one water. A radio technician carries home no relic and writes no book of marvels. He carries a route, and the route is the thing his family hears recited in the last week, in the correct order, from a bed.
suggested_refs: The site of Samudera Pasai near Lhokseumawe, Aceh

stops.name: Colon, the school on the Atlantic side
stops.date_confidence: attested for Noriega and the school, unfixed for Ben: 1966 is the year Noriega was at Fort Gulick, offered as the tightest available hypothesis for an encounter and nothing more
stops.campa: At Fort Gulick, on the Atlantic mouth of the canal near Gatun Lake, the United States runs the School of the Americas until the school is moved to Fort Benning in 1984. Manuel Noriega comes here as a second lieutenant in 1966, four years out of the Chorrillos military school at Lima, and returns later for infantry, counterintelligence, and jungle warfare; he wears the school's crest on his uniform. Juan Peron sat out part of his exile in this same town in 1956, and married there.
suggested_refs: Fort Gulick and the School of the Americas rosters, Canal Zone, 1966

stops.name: Gatun, the locks the Frenchman could not finish
stops.date_confidence: unfixed for Ben; the Eiffel contract of 1887 is attested in its own file
stops.campa: Gustave Eiffel built the locks for the Compagnie Universelle in 1887, and the company went down in fever and fraud before water ever ran through them. The Americans dug the canal a second time and kept the Zone as a strip of their own country cut through somebody else's. Ben, a Navy man among Navy men, passes through a place where two empires left their machinery in the same mud. The essay records no word from him about Panama. The queue records only that he met the man who would come to rule it.
suggested_refs: The Gatun locks and the abandoned French works of the Compagnie Universelle

stops.name: Panama City, the meeting the queue records
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the corpus states the meeting and fixes neither year, place, nor circumstance; every element of this stop except the meeting itself is reconstruction
stops.campa: The queue of the Colegio Invisible states it flatly: he met Manuel Noriega. No date is given, no room, no reason. Noriega will run Panama's intelligence service, take the country in 1983, lose it to an American invasion in 1989, surrender at the Apostolic Nunciature in January 1990, and pass from US custody to French custody in 2010. Between the librarian and the general there is one recorded fact and no circumstance at all. Jose Lopez Rega worked a cabaret in this city in 1955, and Isabel Peron danced her last engagement here that December.
suggested_refs: Noriega's own memoir and the standard Noriega biographies, checked for any US librarian, archivist, or pacifist delegation

stops.name: The Gulf of Tonkin, the traffic that will not stop
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the corpus says war and does not say which; the Vietnam years are reconstruction from his generation and from the pacifism that followed
stops.campa: The war the veterans of his generation came home from is fought in part through men in radio rooms, who take down what is ordered and what results, and who are the first aboard to know both. What happened to Ben is given in the essay as one word, trauma, and the atlas does not go behind the word. He comes off the ship walking with a cane he will use for the rest of his life, carrying on his left shoulder a mark in the shape of a dragon. Nothing in the corpus says how either was got.
suggested_refs: Deck logs of US Navy communications ratings on Yankee Station, 1965 to 1968

stops.name: A naval hospital in the United States (unlocated), the cane and the dragon
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: no discharge date, hospital, or station is attested; the pin is the same declared placeholder as the birth
stops.campa: He is discharged and turns from the fleet to its refusal. The corpus calls him a radical pacifist and names no organization, no march, and no date; the atlas leaves that gap standing open rather than filling it. No discharge paper, hospital, or shore station is attested either, so the pin rests on the same declared placeholder as the birth. The man who spent his working watches transmitting other men's orders spent the rest of his life in the custody of documents nobody was ordering anywhere, and he walked to them with a stick.
stops.quote: In the navy he operated as a radio communications technician, and the trauma he sustained at war left him as a radical pacifist who walked with a cane and carried the mark of a dragon on his left shoulder.
suggested_refs: Membership rolls of the Fellowship of Reconciliation, the War Resisters League, and Vietnam Veterans Against the War, none of which could be searched without his legal name

stops.name: Oxford, matriculation among the medievalists
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the corpus asserts the education; no college, matriculation year, supervisor, or thesis has been found in any public register, and the corpus does not even settle whether Oxford came before the Navy or after it
stops.campa: He reads medieval studies at Oxford. No college, no year, no supervisor, and no thesis title has been found in any public register, and the search that went looking for them ran out of quota and came back with nothing under any combination of the descriptors. The corpus asserts the training and the atlas records the assertion as an assertion. What the training produced is visible later, and is the only evidence for it: a man who says Gaul when he means Gaul.
suggested_refs: Oxford University matriculation registers and the Rhodes Trust scholar rosters, searchable only under his legal name

stops.name: Oxford, the letters made by hand
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: reconstruction of the standard Oxford medieval training of the period
stops.campa: A medievalist is made in reading rooms, at desks where a manuscript arrives on a cradle and goes back at a fixed hour. He learns the disciplines that will be his trade for forty years: catalogue, collate, describe, shelve, retrieve. The order of a library is a memory system with a building around it, and the men who invented the art of memory in antiquity built theirs out of exactly this, rooms with places in them and one fixed route between the places. He is learning a theatre and does not yet know that is what it is.
suggested_refs: Duke Humfrey's Library and the Bodleian manuscript reading room

stops.name: Dublin, Trinity College: the Book of Kells
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the book is named by the dying man; no visit by Ben is attested and the stop stands for the object, not for a documented journey
stops.campa: The Book of Kells lies in the Old Library under glass, four gospels written and painted at Iona or at Kells around the year 800, its carpet pages built out of knotwork that runs unbroken through a whole leaf and comes back to itself. A man trained on such pages has spent years looking at knots that are also arguments. In hospice he speaks of the Book of Kells and of sailor knots in the same breath, and his stepson, working the knots out of his back, does not find that strange.
suggested_refs: The Book of Kells, Trinity College Dublin MS 58, Old Library

stops.name: Narbonne, the last city in Gaul
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the essay names Gaul and does not say whether he travelled there or only read it; the pin is inherited from the atlas's own Gaul
stops.campa: He uses the word Gaul and uses it correctly. Gallia is the Roman and Merovingian country, wider than France, taking in Belgium, the Rhineland, part of Switzerland and Cisalpine Italy, and after the middle of the eighth century the scholars stop writing Gaul and write Francia. Narbonne was the Umayyad forward base in that country, held by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi from 721 and lost to the Franks a generation later. Whether Ben walked there or only read it, the corpus does not say and the atlas will not guess.
suggested_refs: The Merovingian and Carolingian charters of Narbonne and Septimania

stops.name: Sewanee, the Domain and the chief librarian
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: no appointment date is attested; the corpus gives the post and not the year
stops.campa: The University of the South sits on ten thousand acres of the Cumberland Plateau that the school calls the Domain, an Episcopal college with a seminary attached and a library at its middle. Ben takes his post there as librarian and archivist and keeps it for the rest of his working life. No staff list, annual report, or alumni notice naming him has been found in any public search. The corpus is the whole of the evidence, and the corpus calls him the chief librarian.
stops.quote: My stepfather, Arthur Ben, was a dear man, gentle, erudite, a bibliophile, and grand master of library science.
suggested_refs: University of the South staff directories and Sewanee alumni magazine notices

stops.name: Sewanee, the Jessie Ball duPont Library
stops.date_confidence: the building's 1965 opening is attested; Ben's presence in it is corpus testimony placed in sequence
stops.campa: The library opened in 1965, and under its one roof sit two divisions of the same building: the University Archives and Special Collections, and the library of the School of Theology. This is the single room of the journey with a wall around it: the building exists, the archives are in it, and any Sewanee employment described as work at duPont must fall after 1965. Everything else about his post there stands on the family's word, which the atlas takes, and says out loud that it is taking.
suggested_refs: Jessie Ball duPont Library, University Archives and Special Collections, Sewanee
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Sewanee: The University of the South'

stops.name: Sewanee, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: no date or place of marriage is attested anywhere in or out of the corpus
stops.campa: He marries the author's mother and becomes a stepfather, which is the office the corpus knows him in. The essay says he loved her with the romantic heroism, chivalry, and ferocious idiocy of a Lancelot, then says he was also a Merlin, and lets the two stand side by side without settling which one he was. The atlas keeps both. Lancelot rides into this atlas from Comper and the water; Merlin is the other kind of figure entirely, the one who arranges a story he is not himself inside.
suggested_refs: Franklin County, Tennessee marriage records, searchable only under his legal name

stops.name: Sewanee, the Ayat al-Kursi on the children's door
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the essay reports the talisman without a year
stops.campa: He hangs a cloth talisman on the door of the children's bedroom containing the Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse of the second sura, recited across the Muslim world for protection through the night. An Episcopal seminary's archivist hangs Arabic scripture over sleeping American children and nobody in the house writes down an explanation. At the end of his life he will tell their mother that Hebrew and Arabic writing is emerging inside his pancreas and his liver, and that he cannot read what it says.
suggested_refs: Ayat al-Kursi, Qur'an 2:255, in its common use as a hung textile talisman

stops.name: Sewanee, the tablecloth folded at dinner
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: a habit of years, reported without dates
stops.campa: His hands work the cloth at the table in a fixed sequence, vertical then horizontal, doubling and doubling again. The children see it every evening for years as the tic of an orderly man. The essay identifies later what the folding was: a control panel laid out on linen for a memory theatre in which archives are filed and accessed, relics are placed, and elaborate vegetarian banquets are prepared with the utmost care for the ordering of placement. He has been operating it at the dinner table for decades before anyone in the room can see it.
suggested_refs: The ars memorativa from Simonides to Camillo, Bruno, and Fludd, as a professional subject of medieval studies

stops.name: Sewanee, the YMCA studio: the mats side by side
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: dated in the essay only by the stepson's age, six
stops.campa: A slender woman calls the sequence in a studio at the Y, and a man with a cane and a six-year-old boy move through it on mats laid next to each other for nearly an hour, ending on their backs with their eyes closed in the waking sleep the posture is named for. The cane leans against the wall for the length of the class. The boy will not think about the hour again for twenty-five years. It comes back to him whole, in a hospice room, at the moment a knot in his stepfather's back gives way under his fingers.
suggested_refs: The corpse pose, savasana, as taught in American YMCA studios of the period

stops.name: Sewanee, the hospice room
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: no date of death or of admission to hospice has been located; the year is a placement and is not a finding
stops.campa: The family assembles at the bedside. The room fills with something the household's usual explanations do not cover, and the household stops trying to cover it. The dying man's talk goes outward first, through straits and tribes and bloodlines, and then comes back in close, to knots and manuscripts and the libraries he says are underneath them. His stepson writes afterward that in the final passage the chief librarian took on the appearance of Gandalf the White.
stops.quote: The room took on the thick cloud of an arcane fiction, the likes of which the familiar doctrine of historical materialism was ill-suited.
suggested_refs: Hospice and funeral records at Sewanee, Franklin County, Tennessee

stops.name: Sewanee, the sheets folded into a control panel
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: sequence within the last weeks, not a calendar date
stops.campa: The hands that folded the tablecloth now fold the bed sheets, and the same sequence produces the same instrument. He works it from the bed: filing, retrieval, the placement of relics, the setting of a table for guests who are not in the room. As the body fails the operation gets harder, the way an organ gets harder to play with a failing hand rather than a failing memory. The theatre itself does not degrade; the rooms stay where they were put and the route between them holds. What degrades is the access to it.
stops.quote: His sequencing of vertical and horizontal doubling of the cloth created a mantle which formed the control panel of a complex memory theatre.
suggested_refs: Frances Yates, The Art of Memory, on the theatre as an operable instrument rather than a metaphor

stops.name: Ur of the Chaldees, the bloodlines of Abraham
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: a station of the hospice speech, not a journey he made; the pin is the atlas's own Ur
stops.campa: Abram is born at Tell el-Muqayyar in the Chaldean country, goes out at seventy-five, and fathers by two women the lines that both of Ben's talismans belong to: the Hebrew of the phylactery, the Arabic of the Throne Verse. The dying librarian speaks of the bloodlines of Abraham in the same sentence as two sea straits, which is to say he files a genealogy and a shipping lane in adjacent drawers. The Kaaba that Abraham and Ishmael raise stands at the eastern end of the water he sailed.
suggested_refs: Tell el-Muqayyar, the ziggurat of Ur, and the Genesis account of the departure from it

stops.name: The Temple Mount, the apron and the murdered architect
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: a station of the hospice speech; the pin is the canonical Temple Mount of the Hiram and Solomon files
stops.campa: Hiram Abiff dies on this platform in the Masonic legend, struck down by three of his own workmen for a word he will not give up, and Solomon's house is finished without him. Out of that death the lodges take their aprons, plain white lambskin, the badge they call older than the Golden Fleece. Ben asks for an apron. The census of the Colegio Invisible already carries him as a grand master, and the atlas notes that the essay and the census came to that word by different roads and arrived at the same one.
suggested_refs: The Hiramic legend and the lambskin apron of Masonic initiation

stops.name: Paracas, the tunics from the caverns
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: a station of the hospice speech; the pin is the atlas's own Paracas landing
stops.campa: In the necropolis under the Peruvian desert the dead of Paracas were wrapped in embroidered mantles two thousand years before any lodge existed, bundled seated, the cloth carrying the whole cosmology the body was leaving behind. Ben names those tunics and the Masonic apron in one breath, as two entries filed under a single heading: a garment made by hand for a departure. San Martin landed on this coast in 1820 with an army. The dying man lands on it with a specification for a belt.
stops.quote: In great detail he described a funerary belt the likes of a Masonic apron or one of the tunics of the Paracas Caverns.
suggested_refs: The Paracas Cavernas textiles, Museo Nacional de Arqueologia, Lima

stops.name: Paris, the amphitheatre built for the king
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: a station of the hospice speech; the pin is the canonical Paris of the Camillo file
stops.campa: Giulio Camillo built a wooden theatre for Francis I in which the spectator stood on the stage and the seven grades of the world rose in front of him, every image a drawer holding everything sayable about its subject. Viglius inspected the thing at Venice and reported both the amazement and the drawers. Camillo died at Milan in 1544 and the theatre was never found again. Ben, four and a half centuries on, folds one out of bed linen in Tennessee and operates it with his hands until his hands give out.
suggested_refs: Giulio Camillo, L'Idea del Theatro (Florence, 1550)

stops.name: Sewanee, the libraries underneath
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: sequence within the last weeks, not a calendar date
stops.campa: He tells them there are enormous libraries beneath the ground, holding secrets of value. A man who spent forty years above a special collections vault on a mountain in Tennessee says this at the end, and nobody present contradicts him. His talk keeps returning to the knot and to the buried room where what is written is kept out of the weather. Between the two lies the whole of his trade: a thing tied so that it holds, and a place built so that what is tied can be found again.
stops.quote: In his final passage our chief librarian took on the appearance of Gandalf the White, and his stories moved closer to us, navigating descriptions of sailor knots, the Book of Kells, and those valuable secrets held in the giant subterranean libraries beneath us.
suggested_refs: The below-grade stacks and special collections vault of the duPont Library

segments.name: The Second Life in Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the second life told aloud
stops.date_confidence: unfixed, and fictive by the essay's own framing: this is a life imagined for him at the bedside, not a life he lived
stops.campa: The stepson holds his hand and tells him a story about himself in which he lives in Argentina instead, in a city that puts books about books at its center, keeps his library of arcana rather than selling it, and makes friends with Ral Veroni and with Daniel Zachariah, the bookseller of Hershel. Both men are already in the census of the Colegio Invisible, entered out of this same passage. The second life is told aloud to the man it is about, in the room where the first one is ending.
stops.quote: I had been imagining a second life for Ben, one in Argentina and the city of Buenos Aires, where libraries and literature and books about books are placed at the center.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires bookselling world of Ral Veroni and Daniel Zachariah

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the National Library on calle Mexico
stops.date_confidence: unfixed and fictive: the pin belongs to Borges, and stands here for the city Ben is given rather than for any place he went
stops.campa: Jorge Luis Borges was made director of the National Library in October 1955, by which time he could no longer read, and wrote that God had given him at once the books and the night. The city Ben is handed in the story is Borges's city, where a librarian is a public figure and a private catalogue is a form of literature. In the parallel thread the library of arcana is not dispersed. In this one it was sold, and the essay says so in a single clause and does not stop over it.
suggested_refs: The old Biblioteca Nacional on calle Mexico 564, Buenos Aires

stops.name: The pampa, the estancia night read into the room
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: the reading is attested in the essay, the pin is Keyserling's estancia of 1929
stops.campa: The stepson reads aloud from Keyserling, who came to the Argentine campo in 1929, watched an old man dance and the gauchos rope cattle, and wrote the roping as lacemaking and the meal after it as the circle of Penelope's suitors. The family at the bedside has been sitting exactly as Penelope sits, weaving a garment in order to postpone an ending. The book they choose to read into the room is the one that names the same figure back at them from an estancia ninety years earlier.
stops.quote: With the same deftness and deliberation, the same enjoyment of complication and fuss with which the old ladies of my youth were wont to weave delicate laces out of threads fastened to pegs, the animals had been caught by means of lassos cunningly thrown out by the gauchos from various sides, encircling now a horn, now a foot, until the catch stood there motionless.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Keyserling, South American Meditations, read at the bedside; quoted in 200_arthur_ben.md
suggested_refs: Hermann Keyserling, South American Meditations (1932), the chapters on the campo

stops.name: Sewanee, the apron specified
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: sequence within the last weeks, not a calendar date
stops.campa: Alone with the two boys he prompts the construction of the thing he needs for his departure. It is to be hand stitched. It is to have pockets. He describes it in the detail of a man writing a finding aid: dimensions, closure, contents, and the order of the contents. This is the last accession of a forty-year career, and the object being catalogued is the cataloguer. The family takes down the specification and starts to sew, which is what the essay means when it says they sat as Penelope.
suggested_refs: The apron itself, if it survives in the family's keeping

stops.name: Sewanee, the two front pockets
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: sequence within the last weeks, not a calendar date
stops.campa: The two pockets at the front are to hold the ashes of his parents. He was born to them in a town that no public record and no line of the corpus will name, and he means to leave carrying them at his waist, in a garment sewn by hand by his wife's children. The atlas notes what this does to its own first stop. The birth it could not place is not missing after all; it has been moved. A funerary belt is a container before it is a symbol, and this one is loaded before it is ever tied.
suggested_refs: The disposition of his parents' ashes, unrecorded in any reachable source

stops.name: Sewanee, the knot in the likeness of Shin
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: sequence within the last weeks, not a calendar date
stops.campa: The apron ties in front with a knot made in the likeness of Shin, the three pointed crown of the Hebrew letter, the letter the priest's hands make in the blessing and the letter cut into the head of a phylactery. He tells his wife that Hebrew and Arabic writing is emerging inside his pancreas and his liver and that he does not know its meaning. The inscriptions are making a phylactery of him, a fabric talisman with a verse shut inside it, like the one he hung on the children's door.
suggested_refs: The letter Shin on the head-tefillin and in the priestly blessing

stops.name: Sewanee, I need help with my strings
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: sequence within the last weeks, not a calendar date
stops.campa: He reaches his arms out with a grimace and says it plainly, the way a man says a thing about equipment. The strings are in his back. His stepson slides a hand between the body and the bed and finds enormous knots between the fifth and sixth thoracic vertebrae and the shoulder, the left shoulder, the one that carries the dragon. The operator of the theatre is requesting maintenance on the mechanism, and the mechanism is a spine. Nobody in the room treats the request as a figure of speech.
stops.quote: I need help with my strings.
stops.quote_source: 200_arthur_ben.md, the hospice room at Sewanee (locked essay corpus)
suggested_refs: The fifth and sixth thoracic vertebrae, named in the essay with a librarian's precision

stops.name: Sewanee, the knots given one by one
stops.date_confidence: unfixed: sequence within the last weeks, not a calendar date
stops.campa: Breath by breath he presents each knot and presses it against his stepson's fingers, in order, the way he shelved and the way he folded. As they loosen and the channels open one after another there is a rush of memory and the stepson is six years old again on a mat at the Y, moving through a sequence beside him and finishing on his back with his eyes shut. The last thing the librarian files is the finding aid itself, and he hands it over knot by knot to the only pair of hands in the room that can take it.
suggested_refs: Sailor knots and the knotwork of the Book of Kells, named together in the same hospice passage

stops.name: Sewanee, the departure

stops.campa: He dies at Sewanee with the apron made, the pockets loaded, and the knot tied in the shape of a letter. No obituary, no grave marker, and no death notice has been found in the Sewanee Mountain Messenger, in the university's alumni notices, or in any public index, and the search that went looking exhausted itself and came back empty. What survives him in the atlas is one essay, one census line calling him bibliophile and grand master, one queue entry recording that he met Manuel Noriega, and a route through two straits.
